title: Supervision 5 short-answer questions
description: Three short-answer questions (SAQs) on this week’s lectures. They’re for practice, not to hand in.
instructions:
Optional practice. These short-answer questions go with this week’s lectures. Only the essay needs to be handed in, but SAQs are good practice at writing short, focused answers, and they’re good revision too.

  • Each is marked out of five, so answer in bullet points and aim for at least five separate points.
  • There’s no time limit, but about 10 minutes for each is a good aim.
  • Each one can be answered with an equation as its frame. Say which equation, and use it.
  • Answer as many as you like. You can leave some blank and still submit.
  • After you submit, Review my answers shows you the points a good answer covers.

questions.title: Heart rate and cardiac output
questions.text: Explain why increasing heart rate alone does not greatly increase cardiac output.
questions.guidance:
• The frame. CO = HR × SV, but in a steady circulation the cardiac output must equal venous return, VR = (MSFP − RAP) / RvR. The heart can only take blood from the veins as fast as it returns.
  • RAP is already close to zero. A healthy heart keeps the right atrial pressure close to zero, even at rest. Pumping faster can only lower RAP a little further, because the great veins collapse once the pressure in them falls 1 or 2 mmHg below zero. So venous return can’t rise much, each beat fills less, and SV falls as HR rises: CO hardly changes. The heart can’t “pull” blood from the veins.
  • MSFP sets the maximum. The heart can’t change MSFP, which depends on the blood volume and the tone of the veins (the circulation is a closed system).
  • The evidence. Guyton replaced the right heart of dogs with a pump: below normal, less pumping reduced the cardiac output, but more pumping didn’t raise it. Pacing the heart faster doesn’t raise the cardiac output unless venous return is raised too, but an arteriovenous fistula, a short cut back to the heart, shows that the heart can pump much more when more blood returns (Cowley and Guyton, 1971). The cardiac output follows MSFP, not the heart rate (Barnes, Bower and Rink, 1985).
  • For more marks. In Guyton’s curves, raising the heart rate and contractility alone lifts the cardiac function curve, but it meets the venous return curve where it is flat, at a negative RAP, so the output hardly rises. In exercise a faster heart does help, because venoconstriction raises MSFP and the muscle pump lowers RvR at the same time. At very high rates, diastole is so short that filling, and so SV, falls further.

questions.title: Pulse pressure, mean pressure and the baroreflex
questions.text: A healthy person has an arterial blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. Calculate the pulse pressure and estimate the mean arterial pressure. Then outline the reflex responses that would follow a sudden fall in arterial pressure.
questions.guidance:
• Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic = 120 − 80 = 40 mmHg.
  • Mean arterial pressure ≈ diastolic + pulse pressure / 3 = 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg. It’s nearer the diastolic pressure because the pressure spends more of each cycle near it: a brief peak during ejection, then a slow fall through the longer diastole.
  • Detection. The baroreceptors of the carotid sinus (afferents in the glossopharyngeal nerve, IX) and the aortic arch (the vagus, X) are stretched less and fire less. Their signals reach the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla, which now inhibits the vasomotor area less and excites the cardioinhibitory area less. Below about 60 mmHg the arterial chemoreceptors help too.
  • Effectors, within seconds, term by term. With ABP = CO × TPR and CO = VR = (MSFP − RAP) / RvR as the frame: sympathetic constriction of the arterioles (noradrenaline on α1-adrenoceptors) raises TPR; sympathetic venoconstriction raises MSFP, and so venous return and the cardiac output; less vagal and more sympathetic activity (β1) raise the heart rate and contractility, so the extra venous return is pumped; the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline.
  • For more marks. If the fall comes from a loss of volume, the low-pressure receptors of the atria and great veins act through the hypothalamus over longer times (ADH, renal sympathetic activity and thirst) to restore the blood volume and MSFP. The arterial baroreceptors are most sensitive close to the normal mean pressure, and they reset if the mean changes for long.

questions.title: Diving and altitude
questions.text: Explain why breath-hold diving and ascent to altitude produce different cardiovascular responses.
questions.guidance:
• Two different stresses. In a breath-hold dive no O2 comes in at all, so the priority is to make the O2 in the body last, for the brain and the heart. At altitude you can breathe, but each litre of arterial blood carries less O2, so the priority is to deliver more: O2 delivery = flow × concentration, so the flow (the cardiac output) has to rise.
  • The local effect of a low PO₂ is metabolic vasodilatation, which would only let the tissues use up the scarce O2 faster.
  • The primary chemoreceptor response (the diving reflex). The carotid and aortic bodies detect the hypoxia, and the medulla slows the heart (a vagal reflex) and constricts the systemic vessels (sympathetic), overriding the local dilatation. Cardiac work falls, and the blood that flows goes to the brain and the heart, whose vessels have little sympathetic constrictor supply. It’s strong in seals, and it can be seen in humans.
  • The secondary response, at altitude. When breathing is possible, hypoxia makes you breathe faster and deeper. Pulmonary stretch receptors then signal through the vagus to the medulla, causing venoconstriction (a higher MSFP), a faster heart and the release of adrenaline. The cardiac output rises, which makes up for the lower arterial {O2} content. This response to the response overrides the primary one.
  • For more marks. In obstructive sleep apnoea, repeated primary responses to hypoxia during sleep may lead to chronic hypertension.
